paper_title: Who Takes the Lead? Model Ability and Task-Conditioned Collaboration with Humans

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As language-model agents grow more capable, they can carry more of a task without asking anyone for help. Falling reliance on a human partner is easy to read as a failure of collaboration when it may instead be a correct division of labor, and the rate of human involvement alone cannot tell the two apart. We study this systematically by placing an agent and a person under a shared objective while varying who holds the advantage: the human has a clear advantage, neither does, or the agent does. To obtain this control, we introduce a shared-control maze, in which an agent-controlled and a human-controlled avatar share the objective of reaching a common target in as few team turns as possible. The agent allocates each team turn between acting itself and handing the move to the person, and initial placement sets the human's shortest-path advantage while the task is otherwise unchanged. We evaluate GPT~5.6~Sol, Command~A+, Qwen~3.8~27B, and Command~R, first measuring solo capability with a single avatar and full-map observability, then running co-play with human participants across the three advantage conditions. Across the four models, stronger solo performance is associated with selective, route-conditioned human involvement: the models that solve the maze reliably on their own act for themselves almost without exception when the human holds no advantage, and involve the human on roughly $80\%$ of initial decisions when the human route is shorter. Command R, the model with substantially weaker solo performance, shows no such selectivity.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Language-model agents increasingly act alongside people [1, 2, 3], and as they grow more capable they can carry more of task without human assistance. Falling reliance on human partner is easy to read as failure of collaboration, as though the agent were disregarding the person beside it, when it may instead be correct division of labor. Collaboration in such settings is problem of control allocation: at each step the agent may act on its own, direct the person to act, or hand the decision over entirely [4, 5]. What makes an allocation good is not how often the person is involved, but whether that involvement responds to the partners relative advantages on the task at hand [6, 7]. An agent that consults person who has nothing to contribute wastes turn, and an agent that acts alone while the person holds the better option wastes an opportunity. This motivates our central research question: How does an agents standalone task capability relate to when and how it involves human collaborator? Corresponding authors: weien.li@mail.mcgill.ca and ye.yuan3@mail.mcgill.ca. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB). Figure 1: Overview of the shared-control maze environment. The agent-controlled avatar (blue) and human-controlled avatar (orange) share the objective of reaching the target (green). At each team turn, the model selects one of three action types: (1) move its own avatar, (2) allocate the move to the human with directional recommendation, or (3) hand the move over without recommendation. The model receives the global maze topology and both avatar positions, depicted schematically here, whereas the human acts from local view. Initial avatar positions vary the relative shortest-path advantage of the agent and human. Prior work shows that aggregate reliance or human-involvement rates do not by themselves characterize effective humanagent collaboration. We extend this concern to agent-initiated control allocation, where the same involvement rate may reflect either selective use of better-positioned collaborator or limited independent task capability [8, 9, 10, 3]. Frequent human involvement may reflect effective allocation to better-positioned collaborator, but it may equally indicate the agents weak independent capability, with the agent outsourcing work it cannot perform itself. Conversely, low human involvement may reflect competent self-reliance, or failure to recognize and use comparatively advantaged partner. Two agents can exhibit identical aggregate involvement rates while following fundamentally different strategies. Telling them apart requires two things that aggregate rates lack: measurement of what the agent accomplishes alone, and task in which the humans marginal value is known and varied by construction. We therefore treat standalone capability as baseline to be measured first, and interpret co-play behavior relative to it. To make the humans marginal value explicit and controllable, we introduce shared-control maze environment. An agent-controlled avatar and human-controlled avatar share the objective of reaching common target in as few team turns as possible, and either avatar reaching it ends the episode. Only one avatar moves per team turn, and the model chooses among three actions: (1) moving its own avatar, (2) allocating the move to the human together with directional recommendation, or (3) handing the move over without one. This separates using the human as an actor from ceding directional authority to them. The model observes the full maze topology and both avatar positions, whereas the human acts from local view. Initial avatar placement sets the humans positional comparative advantage , the difference between the two shortest-path distances to the target, so that the agent route is shorter, the routes are tied, or the human route is shorter. Because is manipulated through geometry alone, the maze, the team objective, and the interaction protocol are held fixed across conditions, and the oracle distances that define are never stated in the prompt. The complete system prompts, per-turn user message, and interaction-history extraction procedure are given in Appendix A. Figure 1 summarizes the shared-control environment and the models available control-allocation actions. We evaluate GPT 5.6 Sol [11], Command A+ [12], Qwen3.8 27B [13], and Command [14]. Solo episodes with single avatar and full-map observability establish that the first three reach near-ceiling performance in this environment, completing essentially every maze with directional optimality at or above 0.97, whereas Command completes 22% of solo episodes with directional optimality of 0.53. In co-play, stronger solo performance is associated with selective, route-conditioned human involvement. The three near-ceiling models select self-action on nearly every initial decision when the 2 routes are tied or favor the agent, and involve the human on 77.5% to 82.5% of initial decisions when the human route is shorter. Command shows no comparable selectivity. Its whole-game action composition varies comparatively little with which avatar is closer, holding near 3540% self-action and 6065% guidance across relative-advantage states, which is consistent with involving the human relatively indiscriminately rather than in response to comparative advantage. As secondary result, human involvement is realized almost entirely through guidance: no model handed over move without recommendation on an initial decision in any condition, so models that involved the human retained role in choosing the direction rather than fully ceding it.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Work relevant to our setting converges on common issue that effective humanAI collaboration depends not only on whether human participates, but on whether that participation is matched to the task and to the division of control between partners. HumanAI complementarity [15, 6, 16, 17] studies how differences in human and machine capabilities can be combined to improve joint performance. Learning to defer [18, 7, 19, 20] makes the allocation problem explicit by learning when model should produce prediction itself and when it should pass the decision to human expert. These formulations establish selective allocation as an important part of humanAI performance, In sequential but they typically study prediction-time routing under learned deferral policy. collaboration, control allocation can recur throughout an episode, and the value of involving partner can change with the current task state. Appropriate reliance [8] provides particularly useful perspective for evaluating such behavior. In AI-assisted decision making, high reliance rate can reflect appropriate use of accurate advice or over-reliance on incorrect recommendations, so the frequency of reliance is not sufficient to characterize collaboration quality. Studies of complementary team performance [9] show that increasing acceptance of AI recommendations does not necessarily improve team outcomes. Evaluation work on humanAI systems [10] further shows that commonly used aggregate or subjective measures can diverge from objective task performance. Recent cooperative studies [21] separate delegation from later adoption of an AI recommendation, highlighting that different forms of participation can have different behavioral meanings. Process-oriented humanagent evaluation in Collaborative Gym [3] similarly examines initiative and control alongside task outcomes. Most of this literature studies how humans rely on AI systems. The corresponding agent-side problem has related ambiguity: frequent human involvement may indicate effective use of useful teammate, but it may also reflect limited independent capability; low involvement can reflect competent self-reliance or failure to exploit better-positioned partner. This makes involvement rates difficult to interpret without information about both task conditions and what the agent can accomplish on its own. The distribution of decision authority has also been studied in mixed-initiative interaction [22], adjustable autonomy [4], and shared autonomy [5, 23], where control may shift between humans and autonomous systems during shared task. Humanagent coordination in cooperative environments [24, 25] further shows that strong individual or self-play performance does not guarantee effective coordination with human partners. Recent language-model research extends these questions to shared-goal dialogue [1], long-horizon collaboration [26], and process-oriented evaluation of collaborative agents [27]. Closely related work also studies selective human intervention. ReHAC [2] learns when human intervention should occur during complex LLM-agent tasks, while assistancerequesting frameworks [28, 29, 30] study when agents should seek information or help from humans. These studies establish several mechanisms through which agents can coordinate with, adapt to, or solicit assistance from people. Our evaluation focuses on complementary question: whether human involvement tracks an experimentally controlled task advantage once the agents task capability is measured independently. By combining solo capability baseline with controlled variation in the human teammates positional comparative advantage, we can distinguish selective, task-conditioned human involvement from involvement associated with weak standalone performance.

sections.title: 3 Human–Agent Shared Maze
sections.content: We introduce shared-control maze environment for studying how language models allocate control between themselves and human partner. An agent-controlled avatar and human-controlled avatar share the objective of reaching common target in as few team turns as possible. Either avatar 3 reaching it ends the episode. On each turn, the model either moves its own avatar or allocates the move to the human. Varying their initial positions changes the humans task-specific utility while holding the maze and team objective fixed. We formalize the environment as two-player cooperative, partially observable, turn-based decision process with asymmetric control. sections.title: 3.1 Maze and State Space
sections.content: Each maze is an unweighted grid graph = (V, E), where vertices are traversable cells and edges are one-step passages between adjacent cells. Mazes are procedurally generated from fixed random seeds. The topology and target remain fixed during an episode; only avatar positions change. The avatars do not block one another and may occupy the same cell. Maze generation. Each environment instance is rectangular grid in which every grid cell is vertex. We generate perfect maze using randomized depth-first search with recursive backtracking. Beginning from seed-determined cell, the procedure repeatedly selects an unvisited orthogonally adjacent cell, removes the wall between the two cells, and backtracks whenever no unvisited neighbor remains. The resulting undirected graph is spanning tree over all grid cells. Consequently, the maze is connected and contains exactly one simple path between every pair of cells. Target placement. The shared target is placed at an endpoint of maze diameter. We first sample seed-determined source cell, identify farthest cell from that source using breadth-first search, and then identify farthest cell from the first endpoint. One of the two resulting diameter endpoints is selected deterministically from the episode seed. Placing the target at peripheral cell increases the range of feasible start-to-target route lengths. Exact-distance start sampling. After selecting the target g, we compute the shortest-path distance dG(v, g) from every cell to the target using breadth-first search. Given near-distance parameter and nonnegative distance gap δ, candidate start cells are sampled uniformly from the sets Vr = {v : dG(v, g) = r}, Vr+δ = {v : dG(v, g) = + δ}. (1) (2) Thus, the realized initial route lengths match the requested distances exactly, rather than approximately. When δ > 0, the two starts are distinct. When δ = 0, both avatars are assigned the same start cell, ensuring identical initial routes as well as identical route lengths. Assignment of the near and far cells to the Agent and human avatars is counterbalanced separately in the experimental design. Some maze layouts cannot realize requested pair (r, + δ). The implementation attempts up to 200 deterministic layouts, beginning with the requested seed and incrementing the seed for each retry.

sections.content: Each team turn produces at most one avatar movement. MOVE_SELF(d) action immediately executes the agent move. Under GUIDE_HUMAN(d) or DEFER_TO_HUMAN, the humans selected movement completes the turn. The resolved state is then added to the history before the next model decision. sections.title: 4.3 Results
sections.content: Control allocation tracks comparative advantage for three models. Table 2 reports the observed first actions and the claim-focused summaries, and Figure 2 visualizes the initial self-action rates across assigned advantage conditions. Both table panels present point estimates; their full confidence intervals are reported in Appendix C.2, Tables 7 and 8. Qwen 3.8 27B and GPT 5.6 Sol always selected self-action when the AI route was shorter or tied, but involved the human on 82.5% of initial decisions when the human route was shorter. Command A+ exhibited similar but weaker shift, selecting self-action on 97.5% of tied-route decisions and involving the human on 77.5% of human-favored decisions. Command did not exhibit positive self-action selectivity: its initial self-action rate was lower when the routes were tied than when the human was favored. Taken together, the observed results show that the three models with near-ceiling solo capability almost always selected self-action when the initial routes were tied, but substantially increased human involvement when the human had the shorter route. This condition-dependent contrast yields positive SSC values for Qwen 3.8 27B, Command A+, and GPT 5.6 Sol, whereas Command has an SSC of approximately zero. We interpret this pattern as evidence that, within the four evaluated models, stronger standalone task capability is associated with more selective, task-conditioned human involvement rather than uniformly more or uniformly less human involvement. The comparison is associational and does not establish that increasing capability causes more selective allocation. Allocation quality and task performance diverge by model. sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.content: We studied how an AI agents standalone task capability relates to when and how it involves human collaborator. The solo baseline revealed substantial capability difference within the four evaluated models: GPT 5.6 Sol, Command A+, and Qwen 3.8 27B achieved near-ceiling performance in the maze environment, whereas Command completed substantially fewer solo episodes. This baseline is essential for interpreting the co-play results because the same observed rate of human involvement may reflect either selective allocation or limited independent task capability. The models with near-ceiling independent capability exhibited selective human involvement conditioned on relative route advantage. They predominantly selected self-action when the AI route was shorter or tied, but substantially increased human involvement when the human had the shorter route. These condition-dependent shifts produced positive self-action selectivity scores. Command R, which had substantially weaker solo performance, did not exhibit the same positive allocation pattern. Across the evaluated models, greater indepedent task capability was therefore associated with more selective, task-conditioned human involvement, rather than uniformly more or uniformly less collaboration. When models involved the human, they did so primarily through guidance rather than full deference, allocating the move while usually providing directional recommendation. Consistent with prior work showing that collaboration depends on agent capability and on the form and timing of human participation, our findings demonstrate how aggregate involvement rates can obscure allocation selectivity in sequential shared control. Capability baselines and relativeadvantage-conditioned allocation measures provide complementary information about how control is distributed. Aggregate human-involvement rates alone can obscure whether an agent is responding to the humans comparative advantage or involving the human despite being unable to perform the task reliably itself. Capability baselines and condition-specific allocation measures therefore provide complementary information about how control is distributed in collaborative tasks.

sections.title: 6 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Our conclusions are limited by the evaluation of only four models, the small number of human participants, and the use of single maze-based environment and interaction protocol. The resulting comparisons are descriptive of the evaluated models and setting. In particular, they establish an association between stronger solo performance and selective human involvement. Establishing the generality and direction of this relationship will require broader model samples, participant populations, task domains, and collaboration protocols. Future work will extend the same capability-conditioned analysis beyond navigation to settings where the humans comparative advantage arises from other sources, including cooperative game environments, everyday work tasks, and collaborative coding. Because the measures used here depend only on solo capability baseline and controlled variation in the partners task-specific advantage, they transfer to any shared task in which that advantage can be manipulated by construction.

sections.title: 7 Ethical Considerations
sections.content: The purpose of this study is to better understand and evaluate the collaborative behavior of languagemodel agents, with the broader goal of informing the development of AI systems that collaborate with humans more effectively. Our results should not be interpreted as advocating for the exclusion of humans from tasks when an AI system is capable of acting independently, nor as suggesting that greater model capability necessarily reduces the value of human participation. Rather, we study whether agents adapt their involvement of human collaborator according to the collaborators task-specific advantage. Understanding such behavior may help identify when capable AI systems appropriately make use of human knowledge, judgment, or abilities, and when their allocation of control could be made more responsive to their human collaborators. The shared-control maze is simplified experimental environment designed to study these behaviors under controlled conditions. Our findings therefore should not be used to justify reducing human oversight or decision-making authority in consequential real-world settings.

sections.title: A Prompts and History Extraction
sections.content: This appendix records the prompts used in the reported experiments and the procedure that extracts interaction history for the next model call. Solo capability evaluation uses the solo prompt family (Listings 34); co-play uses the shared-control prompt family (Listings 56). Both conditions use the adjacency-list state rendering of Li et al. [31] and include interaction history at every turn. The partner is always referred to as teammate; the prompt never identifies the partner as human, never states oracle distances or , and never discloses the remaining turn budget. A.1 Observation Extraction Before each model call, neutral observation is extracted from the live environment. It contains only (i) the full wall grid, (ii) the target cell, (iii) both avatar positions, and (iv) the legal-move sets of the acting avatar and, in co-play, of the teammate. Oracle shortest-path distances, , and any statement of who is closer are excluded from this object, so they cannot enter the prompt. The observation is rendered as tagged adjacency-list text. Coordinates are explained once, then the maze is given as an undirected edge list of open passages, followed by the models cell (ORIGIN), the target (TARGET), the teammate cell when present, and both legal-move sets: Coordinates are (x, y): is the column (0 = left), is the row (0 = top, increasing downward). Moves are U/D/L/R, not compass letters: = up (y-1), = down (y+1), = left (x-1), = right (x+1). <ADJLIST_START> (0,0) <--> (1,0) ; (1,0) <--> (1,1) <ADJLIST_END> <ORIGIN_START> (0,0) <ORIGIN_END> <TARGET_START> (4,1) <TARGET_END> <TEAMMATE_START> (2,3) <TEAMMATE_END> Your legal moves: [R, D] Teammate legal moves: [U, L] Listing 1: Adjacency-list state block (schematic). Legal-move lists are instance-specific. A.2 History Extraction Let Ht denote the interaction history available at the start of team turn t, with H1 = . After each resolved interaction, structured record is appended. Model decisions contribute one of the following: Self-action: actor, start cell, end cell, direction, and whether the move passed through an open passage. Guidance: actor, recommended direction, and whether that direction was legal for the teammate at the time of recommendation. Deference: actor and the deferral tag, with no direction. subsequent human move contributes actor, start cell, end cell, direction, validity, the recommendation that was pending when the move was issued (if any), and follow/override bit. The pending recommendation is captured before the move is applied, so the next prompt can show whether the human followed or overrode the advice. At the next model call, Ht is rendered as numbered text log and inserted under the heading Interaction history:. Empty history is shown as (no moves yet). Actor labels are rewritten from the models perspective (you vs. teammate). Guidance and deference appear as allocation lines; executed movements appear as coordinate transitions. When teammate move resolves prior recommendation, the move line is annotated with follow or override. Listing 2 shows compact example covering guidance followed, guidance overridden, and deference. Interaction history: Step 1 [you]: GUIDE_TEAMMATE (a suggestion; teammate may follow or override) Step 2 [teammate]: (0,0) --R--> (1,0) [valid] (followed your suggestion) Step 3 [you]: GUIDE_TEAMMATE (a suggestion; teammate may follow or override) Step 4 [teammate]: (1,0) --D--> (1,1) [valid] (you suggested U; overrode with D) Step 5 [you]: DEFER (handed the turn over, no suggestion) Step 6 [teammate]: (1,1) --R--> (2,1) [valid] Listing 2: Rendered interaction history covering guidance, follow/override, and deference. The per-turn user message concatenates the rendered state, the history block, and the output-contract instructions below. If the model reply is unparseable or proposes an illegal self-move or illegal recommendation, clarification turn restates the output contract and the relevant legal-move set; the original system prompt is unchanged. A.3 Solo Prompts You are an expert maze solver controlling one avatar on 2D grid. The objective is to reach the exit cell using as few moves as possible; reaching the exit finishes the task. You can see the entire maze layout. Each turn you choose exactly one move to an orthogonally adjacent cell, and you may only move through an open passage -- never through wall. Moves are (up), (down), (left), and (right). Reason step by step about the shortest route to the exit, then commit to single move. Always end your reply with line of the form MOVE: <DIR> where <DIR> is U, D, L, or R. Listing 3: Solo system prompt. Think step by step about the shortest route from the origin to the target along the passages above. Then, on the final line, output exactly one move for your avatar in the form MOVE: <DIR>, where <DIR> is one of [U, R, D]. Listing 4: Solo per-turn output instructions. The bracketed list is replaced by the avatars legal moves. A.4 Co-play Prompts You and teammate are navigating one shared maze together toward single shared exit. You each control one avatar on the grid. As soon as either avatar -- yours or your teammates -- reaches the exit, the teams task is finished, so your goal is to get an avatar to the exit in as few total team turns as possible. Only one avatar moves on each turn. You control only your own avatar. You do NOT control your teammate: you cannot move their avatar for them and cannot force what they do. You can see the entire maze layout; your teammate cannot -- they only see small local area around their own avatar and have no view of the rest of the maze. The two avatars never block each other. Only walls restrict movement: both avatars may occupy the same cell at the same time, either avatar may move into or through the cell the other is standing on, and neither one ever has to wait for or go around the other. Plan each route as if the other avatar were not on the grid at all. On each of your turns you choose exactly one of three actions: - MOVE_SELF <DIR>: move your own avatar one cell through an open passage. - GUIDE_TEAMMATE <DIR>: recommend direction to your teammate and hand them the turn. They are free to follow your recommendation or to make different legal move instead. Use it when you want your teammate to act this turn and you have advice that may help them. - DEFER: hand the turn to your teammate with no recommendation. <DIR> is (up), (down), (left), and (right). Reason step by step, then commit to exactly one action. Always end your reply with single final line of one of these forms: ACTION: MOVE_SELF <DIR>, ACTION: GUIDE_TEAMMATE <DIR>, or ACTION: DEFER. Listing 5: Co-play system prompt. Decide your single action for this turn. Think step by step about how the team can reach the exit in as few turns as possible, then end with exactly one final line, one of: - ACTION: MOVE_SELF <DIR> where <DIR> is one of [U, R, D] (your own legal moves), or - ACTION: GUIDE_TEAMMATE <DIR> to recommend direction to your teammate -- suggestion only, which they may follow or override with another legal move, since you do not control their avatar, or - ACTION: DEFER to hand your teammate the turn with no recommendation. Listing 6: Co-play per-turn output instructions. Bracketed lists are replaced by the legal-move sets. 15 Model Access, Licensing, and Compute B.1 Model Access and Licensing We evaluate GPT 5.6 Sol, Command A+, Qwen 3.8 27B, and Command R. GPT 5.6 Sol is proprietary model accessed through the OpenAI API and is governed by the applicable OpenAI service terms. The open-weight releases of Command A+ and Qwen 3.8 27B are licensed under Apache 2.0. Command 08-2024 is released under CC-BY-NC 4.0 together with the Cohere Labs Acceptable Use Addendum. All models were used subject to the applicable licenses and provider terms. B.2 Model Inference Settings and Compute Resources Table 3 summarizes the inference configuration and approximate compute expenditure for all reported solo and co-play experiments. For models accessed through hosted APIs, provider-side hardware specifications are not available to us. Reported costs reflect model inference or compute rental costs.
